snippet.title: Used Solar Panels? Do THIS First
snippet.description:
Used solar panels can be a great deal, but before you install them, you need to inspect, clean, repair, and test them.

* Clean the panel

* Decide whether to use it, sell it, or scrap it

snippet.title: Doesn’t like how they look?
snippet.description:
with metallurgical-grade silicon mined primarily from quartz deposits. That quartz gets refined to polysilicon at temperatures exceeding 2,000°F, often using the Siemens process, where trichlorosilane gas is purified to semiconductor-grade silicon with impurity levels measured in parts per billion.

From there, monocrystalline ingots are grown using the Czochralski crystal-growth process. A seed crystal is slowly pulled from molten silicon while rotating, aligning billions upon billions of silicon atoms into a nearly perfect crystal lattice.

Then things get weird.

Small variations in boron, phosphorus, gallium, oxygen content, crystal defects, grain boundaries, wafer thickness, anti-reflective coating deposition, and electron mobility can slightly alter how each cell interacts with different wavelengths of sunlight.

Manufacturers then use electroluminescence imaging, IV curve tracing, spectral response testing, and color sorting algorithms to group cells with similar electrical characteristics and visual appearance before they’re assembled into a module.

The blue color you’re seeing isn’t actually blue. It’s mostly the result of silicon nitride anti-reflective coatings engineered at the nanometer scale to reduce photon reflection and maximize electron excitation across the P-N junction.

In other words, you’re looking at a giant collection of carefully organized sand that has been chemically manipulated, crystallographically aligned, electrically doped, spectrally optimized, and quantum-mechanically encouraged to produce electricity.

And sometimes one panel ends up slightly darker than the one next to it
